# Records that outrun their witnesses

Whoever relies on an agent-produced record later — an auditor, a
researcher, the producer's own future systems — needs a way to check
it that does not depend on having watched it being made. The Axiom
Foundation's software agents encode statutes into executable rules;
people review samples and deterministic gates decide what merges, and
no person witnesses every record at the rate agents produce them. The
records that carry that work — signed rule corpora, the release
histories behind them, the gate declarations that admitted them — are
this paper's subject, and the foundation maintains the receipt package
that checks them. Two production systems outside the foundation built
much of the machinery first; they enter as extraction sources and
adopters where their evidence appears (@sec-extraction,
@sec-adoption).

The question descends from the cryptographic audit-log literature:
secure logs protect past entries after compromise and make append-only
consistency auditable [@Schneier1999SecureAuditLogs;
@Crosby2009TamperEvidentLogging]. This setting asks the
consumer-side version: how an outside verifier checks a complete
agent-produced record corpus from retained repository evidence.

One term needs defining before the threat model. "Custody" here means
cryptographically checkable continuity of a record set — integrity,
authorship by pinned key, witnessed existence by time, append-only
history. Digital forensics uses the same word for something else: a
documented chronology of which people and organizations possessed
evidence and when [@Kent2006ForensicTechniques]. The checks in this
paper identify no human handlers and no transfers of possession; they
mechanize the record-integrity portion of that broader discipline,
and nothing more.

This paper treats the producer's repositories, CI configuration, key
settings, and self-operated monitoring as non-independent trust
inputs: the producer can reconfigure each of them, so under this
threat model none of them alone can establish custody for an outside
verifier.

The receipt package takes the custody route. The producer writes
verifiable records as it works — chained manifests, timestamp tokens,
signatures, attestations — and a verifier with a clone of the
repository later checks the saved evidence against trust anchors the
verifier committed in its own code. The paper makes three
contributions: it states precisely what a composed offline check of
agent-produced records establishes and refuses to establish
(@sec-guarantees, @sec-design); it catalogs the four evidence classes
under which production verification machinery moved into one package,
with the evidence published (@sec-extraction); and it reports the
adoption pattern and the corpus-verification design that extends
custody to published rule corpora (@sec-adoption), placing the package
among adjacent integrity systems (@sec-related).

# What a verifier can conclude {#sec-guarantees}

Four checks cover the record surface. The verifier composes them;
each conclusion is conditional on the specification, trust material,
and options the verifier itself supplied, and each check refuses
rather than warns when its evidence falls short [@receipt-repo].

**Append-only history.** The release-chain verifier, run with its
default options, establishes a contiguous, content-addressed,
producer-signed manifest history from genesis to head whose recorded
state matches the working tree. Supplying a trusted base reference
strengthens the conclusion: every release file present at that
ancestor still carries identical bytes and file mode. The append gate
gives its strongest conclusion the same way — with a base reference
and a data-surface change, a candidate tree extends the trusted ledger
exactly: prefix retained, rows valid, releases untouched, and any
ledger append paired with exactly the next release set.

**Witnessed time.** Each accepted RFC 3161 token [@rfc3161]
establishes that the record existed no later than the token's signed
time, under the consumer's timestamp-authority assumptions: the
verifier checks the token cryptographically against the pinned root
certificates, policy identifiers, and signer identities in the
consumer's specification, for every anchor that specification
configures. The claim is time-bounded, not rewrite-proof: nothing ties
a token's signed time to the record's claimed creation time from
above, so a producer who regenerates, re-signs, and re-witnesses an
entire chain passes a first-contact check — what the tokens then bound
is the regeneration date, not the original history. Rewriting any
release after its witnessed bound is detectable; wholesale
regeneration before first contact is not, which is why the
trust-on-first-use recipe matters (@sec-scope). A witness may record
an authority as unavailable with a reason; the verifier treats that as
a verified declaration of unavailability, never as proof from that
authority — and in the witness lane that acceptance is total: a
witness declaring every authority unavailable verifies with zero
tokens, a producer-writable downgrade of the time layer that the
stricter release-chain lane (which requires the configured token files
themselves) does not share. Consumers who need a floor state one in
policy.

**Producer signatures.** Ed25519 signatures verify against public keys
whose fingerprints live in the verifier's committed specification.
Keyrings support N-of-M thresholds over a domain-separated payload and
explicit legacy generations: callers exclude retired keys for new
material with `allow_legacy=False` and may enable them for immutable
history with `allow_legacy=True`, and malformed or mispinned key
material fails the check outright rather than being skipped in favor
of a sibling key that happens to verify. The strictness is
key-directional: a missing or malformed per-key *signature* counts as
absent, and the check still passes if enough other keys satisfy the
threshold — so corrupting signature files degrades a keyring to its
threshold minimum without refusing.

**Workflow provenance.** For commits touching a protected tree, the
attestation check establishes that GitHub's attestation service
accepted the canonical subject for that commit under an anchored
workflow identity. This check imports a different trust model than
the other three: GitHub is a trusted third party for it, and its
attestations ride Sigstore's machinery — Fulcio-issued certificates
binding OIDC workflow identities, with transparency-log evidence
[@Newman2022Sigstore] — delegated through the GitHub CLI, the
package's one networked call. The anchored identity is a workflow
path and ref; the producer controls that workflow's content. Callers
compose the provided helpers (protected-history enumeration,
enforcement epochs) into a full-history sweep; the package supplies
the pieces, not a single spanning call.

The 0.5.0 release adds a fifth layer [@receipt-pr14]: a closed-world binding between a witnessed
journal and the configured corpus — within the specification's content
roots, an unlisted file, a missing file, a rewritten byte, or a symlink
where a regular file was recorded each refuses, as do two listed paths
that collide under Unicode normalization or case folding and a bound
file whose identity changes while verification runs — and a spanning
`receipt verify` command that runs custody, binding, and
declaration-completeness passes in order, stopping at the first
failure. Its verdict is fail-closed in the strict sense the verifier
documents: pass only if every stage completed and every
required declaration was found; anything else — an exception the
verifier did not anticipate, a verdict it cannot render — is a
failure. The command renders
what it did not establish just as plainly — that any declared gate
actually passed, that encoded rules read the law correctly, or that
the presented history is the only one the producer maintains.

## What a verdict is evidence of {#sec-evidence-value}

A passing verdict is authentication-supporting technical evidence
about the presented clone: integrity of the record set, authorship by
the pinned keys, existence of each recorded prefix no later than its
tokens' signed times, and (with a base reference) preservation of
every release object present at a trusted ancestor. It is not evidence of handler custody in the
forensic sense (@sec-guarantees defines the difference), not evidence
that the history is unique (@sec-scope), not evidence of content
correctness, and not evidence of freshness. Two properties serve a
verifier who must defend a verdict to someone else: the verifier
prints the specification digest and the chain head digest, so an
assessment can quote exactly which policy produced which verdict over
which bytes; and the differential harnesses ship with their rerun
commands and pins, so the tool's error behavior is itself examinable —
the questions any serious challenge to a verification tool asks.
The verifier must also be verifiable: releases publish to PyPI with
provenance, and a consumer pins the package version in committed code
alongside the specification that pins everything else.

# Why the shape follows from the threat {#sec-design}

Each design rule answers a specific way verification could quietly
come to depend on the producer.

**Trust anchors live in the verifier's committed code.** Key
fingerprints, timestamp-authority roots, policy identifiers, content
roots, and required declarations sit in a specification the consumer
commits and reviews. The package ships no defaults: no configuration
surface a producer could preload, no environment variable a deployment
could override. The caller always supplies signing keys; the package
neither stores key material nor reads trust configuration from the
environment.

**Rotation is loud.** Replacing a key is a reviewed change to the
consumer's repository that moves the retired key into an explicit
legacy generation, and the caller chooses per call whether legacy
generations may vouch at all. There are no time-based transition
windows in which either key silently works.

**Verification of saved evidence runs offline on commodity tools.** A
clone, Python, OpenSSL, and Git suffice for the chain, time, and
signature checks, so they work against a producer whose infrastructure
is unavailable — or untrustworthy — at verification time. The
workflow-attestation check is the explicit exception: it queries
GitHub, and the package's differential evidence for that surface is
scoped accordingly (@sec-extraction).

**Specified gaps refuse.** Missing witnesses, malformed rows, unknown
keys, out-of-range times, unlistable directories, paths that escape
the configured roots: the verifiers refuse each with a typed error.
On the ported surfaces the refusal text is the production system's
own, preserved through extraction; the corpus surface ships a
new refusal battery with the same posture. The libraries own no
stdout or stderr; callers render acceptance and refusal, and exit
codes carry the verdict.

# The machinery {#sec-machinery}

Together the six modules shipped through 0.4.0 verify a record set's
history, timing, and authorship from saved evidence; the API reference
at [axiom.org/receipt/api](https://axiom.org/receipt/api/) documents
their public interfaces.

| Module | A pass establishes |
|---|---|
| `canonical` | One byte stream per value: canonical JSON with UTF-16 code-unit key order and ECMAScript number formatting, byte-compatible with the producer's TypeScript implementation. |
| `release_chain` | With default options: a contiguous, content-addressed, producer-signed, witness-receipted manifest history matching recorded state; with a trusted base reference: byte-and-mode identity for every release file present at that ancestor. |
| `append_gate` | With a base reference and a data-surface change: a candidate tree extends the trusted ledger exactly — prefix retained, rows valid, releases untouched, appends paired with exactly the next release set. Without a base reference, full-file invariants only. |
| `sign` | Raw Ed25519 signatures over exact bytes; N-of-M thresholds over a domain-separated payload under consumer-pinned keyrings, with legacy generations governed by the caller's `allow_legacy` choice. |
| `tsa` | One RFC 3161 token matches one consumer-pinned anchor — root bytes, policy, imprint, signed time, signer identity — via OpenSSL; witness sidecars follow the trust-bundle transition rules. |
| `attest` | GitHub's attestation service accepted the canonical subject for a commit under an anchored workflow identity; helpers enumerate protected-tree history and its enforcement epoch for callers to compose. |

The 0.5.0 release adds `corpus` (the closed-world journal binding
and gate-declaration parsing), `verify` (the spanning pass ordering),
and `cli` (`receipt verify`, with text and JSON rendering and
meaningful exit codes) [@receipt-pr14].

# How the machinery earned its way in {#sec-extraction}

The machinery predates the package. The Axiom Foundation's signed
statute corpus supplied key-rotation semantics that the package
adapted and tested [@axiom-corpus-431]; two production systems outside
the foundation supplied the ported verifier surfaces — Chronicle's
release chain [@ledger-repo] and the Thesis Institute's pre-registered
forecast records [@brier-repo], whose preregistration preserves the
prediction-versus-postdiction distinction [@Nosek2018Preregistration]. Extraction, rather than reimplementation,
preserved what the harnesses could hold it to: on the ported surfaces,
the refusal behavior of verifiers that had already caught real
mistakes in production, to the extent the differential batteries
exercise it. Four evidence classes cover everything in the package,
and the evidence for each class is published.

**Byte-identical port.** The canonical-JSON module is the ledger's
file, verbatim: a test pins its SHA-256 against the recorded upstream
hash, so equivalence is identity.

**Differential extraction against the unmodified source verifier.**
The release-chain and append-gate surfaces (from the ledger) and the
witness and attestation surfaces (from the forecast system) came
across behind differential harnesses in the differential-testing
tradition [@McKeemanDifferential]. Each harness pins the upstream
source files by SHA-256, runs the unmodified upstream verifier as an
oracle on live production fixtures — the forecast fixture carries 53
snapshots, 52 available witnesses, and 91 real timestamp tokens; the
witness candidate is a harness-local composition of the package's
modules rather than a whole-script port — and
requires the package to reproduce the oracle's verdicts, accepted and
refused alike, down to message bytes after two disclosed
normalizations (surrounding whitespace and volatile OpenSSL
error-queue identifiers). At the current review head the four
harnesses run 94 cases, all passing.^[Local run at commit `8c5570c`,
2026-08-13: 36 release-chain, 21 append-gate, 17 witness, and 20
attestation differential tests. The attestation harness compares
command construction and outcome handling against a local `gh` stub
and claims no live-network equivalence; the witness harness documents
its exclusions in the test file.] The extraction-time record is also
published: the 633-line release-chain port diff with its review
records, and the 695-line append-gate diff with a review that
sabotaged base-tree materialization and watched 4 of 17 differential
cases fail — evidence that the harness binds the base-tree behavior
it claims to bind [@receipt-receipts]. The reviewer in those records is a
second frontier model lane the maintainers commissioned and ran
adversarially; it is independent of the model that wrote the ports,
not of the organization, and the published record lets a reader weigh
that for themselves. The maintainers are also the producers whose
records the package checks; the verifier-held-anchors design is the
structural answer to that conflict, and this paper's claims are
stated so a reader can check each against the repositories rather
than take the authors' word.

**Semantic adaptation of a production incident.** The signing module's
legacy-generation semantics come from the statute corpus, which
learned them the expensive way: rotating a release key had made
previously published, immutable releases unverifiable
[@axiom-corpus-431]. The fix — retired keys keep verifying the history
they signed, only the current generation signs anything new, malformed
key material is always fatal — entered the package as a design
adaptation with direct tests and no differential oracle.

**New composition.** The corpus binding, spanning verifier,
and CLI are new code composed from the extracted parts. They add no
cryptography and no trust anchors of their own; their evidence is a
refusal battery over the closed-world binding rules, and every guard
carries a regression test that fails with that guard removed
[@receipt-pr14].

The published evidence is uneven in exactly the way the classes
predict, and the repository states which is which: the ledger lane has
raw port diffs, pinned hashes, and independent static reviews; the
forecast lane has pinned hashes and maintained differential harnesses
but no raw port diff; the rotation semantics trace through the pull
requests that carried them (receipt's own and the corpus incident's
[@axiom-corpus-431]) rather than a receipts-directory artifact.

# Adoption {#sec-adoption}

Inside the foundation, the encoder pins the package for the threshold
keyring check on its apply manifests, and the 0.5.0 release extends the same custody discipline to a published
rule corpus; the New Zealand pilot pull request, open as of this
writing, commits a verification specification — custody key, two
timestamp-authority anchors, content roots, required declarations —
and a witnessed journal of 104 rows binding 80 content files, 7
digest-pinned paths, and 17 gate declarations, so an auditor can run
one offline command over a clone and get a fail-closed verdict
[@rulespec-nz-104]. One rule governs what that verdict means to an
outsider: the specification in the producer's repository is the
producer's *proposal*. Verified against it as found, the verdict
establishes internal consistency with a producer-shipped policy;
independent custody requires the auditor to read the specification
once and pin it — at minimum its printed digest — in the auditor's own
records, after which every later check runs against anchors the
producer cannot swap. The specification is executable Python by
design; auditors treat reading it as part of that one-time review, and
an inert data format is candidate future work. Gate rows are
declarations: the verifier proves they were made and bound,
and states plainly that it did not rerun them; declarations concern
the subject commit, and the pilot documents which event-context
outcomes do not transfer across the journal's own publication commit.

As of August 13, 2026, three codebases pin released versions of the
package and call it from their verification paths — code-level
adoption, checkable at each pin, and stated here at exactly that
strength:

| Adopter | Branch | Pin | Surface called |
|---|---|---|---|
| Axiom encoder | default | `receipt==0.3.0` | threshold keyring check on apply manifests |
| Thesis Institute forecast tooling | default | `receipt==0.3.0` (custody extra) | signature primitives in verifier and signer |
| Chronicle | custody branch (unmerged) | `receipt==0.2.0` | release-chain and append-gate shims, differential harnesses re-run on package change |

No adopter yet pins 0.4.0 or the just-published 0.5.0; the
receipt repository's own README states that the observation ledger
consumes the package in production, a producer claim this paper
reports without independent runtime observation.

# Related systems {#sec-related}

receipt assembles per-consumer custody policy in committed code,
multi-anchor timestamp composition, record-level history checks, and
(since 0.5.0) closed-world corpus binding under one
fail-closed verdict that names its non-conclusions. Each neighboring
system solves an adjacent problem, and several share individual
features; the differences below are checkable against their
specifications.

**Timestamping.** Linked timestamping begins with Haber and Stornetta
[@Haber1991Timestamp]; RFC 3161 [@rfc3161] defines the single-token
transaction receipt builds on, and the package composes saved tokens
from the consumer's configured authorities with pinned roots,
policies, and signer identities. OpenTimestamps [@Todd2016OpenTimestamps]
anchors existence in a blockchain instead of pinned authorities — the
principal alternative trust model for witnessed time. Evidence Record
Syntax [@RFC4998; @RFC6283] is the standards answer to keeping such
evidence valid across hash and certificate obsolescence; receipt has
no renewal protocol yet (@sec-scope).

**Transparency logs.** Certificate Transparency [@rfc9162] puts TLS
certificates in public append-only logs with third-party monitors, and
the Go checksum database [@Cox2019GoChecksumDatabase] applies the
pattern ecosystem-wide with client-pinned keys and gossip; receipt
verifies a repository-local history against consumer pins without a
log service, accepting one cost the log systems exist to remove — a
single clone cannot expose a split view. IETF SCITT [@rfc9943;
@microsoftpyscitt2026] registers signed statements with transparency
services that return countersigned inclusion proofs — proofs the
architecture itself calls receipts; SCITT is an online registration
protocol with a service in the loop, where this package checks a
locally held history with no service. PeerReview
[@Haeberlen2007PeerReview] holds distributed nodes accountable by
replaying their tamper-evident logs; receipt never replays or
adjudicates the agent's behavior, only the custody of what it wrote.

**Update and signing systems.** The Update Framework [@tuf-spec;
@Samuel2010Survivable] also roots trust client-side with thresholds
and offline root keys, but is an updater protocol for fetching current
metadata; receipt checks an already obtained clone's history and
rotates roots only through the consumer's reviewed specification.
Sigstore's default keyless flow [@Newman2022Sigstore] binds signatures
to OIDC identities via short-lived certificates and a transparency
log, its bundles verify offline, and it supports self-managed keys;
receipt's signature and witness surfaces use no identity federation
and no log, pinning identities in each consumer's specification —
while its workflow-provenance check explicitly rides GitHub's
Sigstore-backed attestation service as a trusted third party
(@sec-guarantees). Signed Git commits [@gitformat-signature]
authenticate commit objects under locally configured trust, including
a repository-relative allowed-signers file; receipt additionally
verifies the domain-specific chain, witnessed time, historical file
bytes and modes, and corpus binding.

**Process attestation.** in-toto [@TorresArias2019InToto] verifies
that supply-chain steps matched an owner-signed layout, records the
materials and products passed to its tooling, and derives coverage
from the authored rules — with Witness and Archivista as its capture
and storage tooling; receipt verifies custody of the records
themselves and treats process gates strictly as declarations it never
reruns. SLSA [@slsa-spec] specifies leveled requirements rather than
mandating one verifier; receipt is a concrete verifier a consumer
points at one history. Reproducible builds [@reproducible-builds]
compare independently rebuilt artifacts byte for byte; receipt's
differential harnesses compare verifier verdicts on common fixtures,
a related but distinct discipline.

**Agent-record neighbors, and the word "receipt".** The term now
names several adjacent mechanisms. Obsigna's agent receipts
[@obsigna2026] sign and chain individual runtime actions under a
daemon-held key; halo-record [@halorecord2026] captures an agent
event stream with hash chaining and optional RFC 3161 checkpoints;
Basu's tool receipts [@Basu2026ToolReceipts] HMAC-authenticate one
tool observation inside a trusted live runtime for hallucination
checking; and C2PA 2.4's repository receipt [@C2PA2026ContentCredentials]
binds asset ingestion proofs under its X.509 ecosystem. Each
authenticates machine-produced evidence at the event or asset level
inside or against a runtime trust domain; this package verifies the
durable repository history those events could land in, under trust
policy each consumer commits — runtime grounding records and
repository custody compose rather than compete. Richer agent
provenance schemas [@Souza2025PROVAgent], research-object packaging
[@SoilandReyes2022ROCrate], and proofs of agent computation
[@Wang2026zkAgent] occupy the same neighborhood: description, packaging,
and execution-correctness respectively, each combinable with custody
of the resulting records.

# Scope and pending work {#sec-scope}

A pass establishes custody, not truth: the verifier recognizes gate
declarations but does not rerun them, and nothing in a verdict says
encoded rules read the law correctly. An honestly witnessed stale
clone can pass; a base reference proves the release objects present at
the specified ancestor are unchanged — objects added later sit outside
that claim — and freshness requires an out-of-band expectation.
The practical recipe for both the freshness and regeneration limits is
trust on first use: record the chain head digest and witness times at
first contact, and supply that ancestor as the base reference in every
later check — after which rewriting or regenerating anything the
verifier has once seen refuses. Equivocation — a producer maintaining
parallel histories for different verifiers — sits outside what any
single clone can detect; verifiers who compare head digests out of
band get split-view detection for the cost of a message, and the
transparency-log literature (@sec-related) supplies the systematic
version. Consumers configure timestamp-authority diversity; the
verifier enforces the configured anchor set and cannot prove that
authorities fail independently, validates certificates as of the
token's signed time via OpenSSL without revocation checking, and has
no long-term renewal protocol for aging evidence [@RFC4998] — nor
legacy generations for timestamp-authority signers, so an authority's
own key rotation currently splits verification into eras the consumer
spec must carry explicitly. The release-chain lane requires the exact
configured receipt set, so a single configured authority's outage
blocks release publication until the consumer revises policy — the
witness lane's declared-unavailable escape (@sec-guarantees) does not
exist there. The differential harnesses cover finite fixture and
mutation batteries — each test file documents its commands, source
pins, and exclusions, which is also the rerun recipe — not all
possible inputs, and the package inherits the standard assumptions of
its primitives: signature schemes and hash functions unbroken,
timestamp authorities honest about time. Key compromise before
rotation defeats the signature layer for the compromised generation.
The package verifies; it does not yet produce — manifests, witnesses,
and journals come from the producers' own tooling, and a
producer-side reference implementation plus an inert specification
format are the two pieces a second organization would most need. The
waiver ratchet and chronology tiers remain in their source systems
pending extraction. The package is Python; producers on other stacks interoperate
at the artifact layer (canonical JSON, manifests, tokens, signatures)
rather than the library layer.

# Availability

`receipt` is on PyPI (Apache-2.0), with source, port diffs, review
records, and differential harnesses at
[github.com/TheAxiomFoundation/receipt](https://github.com/TheAxiomFoundation/receipt),
the package page at [axiom.org/receipt](https://axiom.org/receipt),
and the API reference at
[axiom.org/receipt/api](https://axiom.org/receipt/api/).
